newsitem.title: USA: Venezuela lands new buyers with light sweet crude.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela lands new buyers with light sweet crude.

text.p: Venezuelan state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), already a top supplier on the crude-thirsty U.S. Gulf Coast, is cracking open new markets with growing exports of sweet Santa Barbara crude oil, traders say.
Most Venezuelan grades tend toward the heavier end of the crude spectrum and are high in sulfur and metals, qualities which make them difficult to refine and market.
In contrast, Santa Barbara is a light grade with low sulfur and metals content that's turning heads on the Gulf Coast, traders say.
"The Venezuelans have made the rounds and it's running all over the Gulf Coast," a U.S. refiner says.

PDVSA subsidiary Corpoven, which has been marketing the new crude since its introduction about one year ago, now sells about four or five spot cargoes, or about two to 2.5 million barrels, per month. This is expected to rise to six cargoes, or three million barrels a month, by the end of the year.
Santa Barbara appeals to refiners that process other sweet crudes such as Colombia's popular Cusiana and North Sea Brent, traders say.
"It may not be as good as Cusiana and Brent, but it's a runnable crude, and it's cheaper," the U.S. refiner says.

Santa Barbara has an American Petroleum Institute gravity of around 35 degrees and contains 0.6 percent sulfur, compared to Cusiana's lighter 36.3 degrees and "sweeter" 0.25 percent sulfur. North Sea competitor and world benchmark Brent crude is lighter still at 38.3 degrees, with 0.37 percent sulfur.

Santa Barbara is now quoted around $1.20 a barrel under benchmark West Texas Intermediate/Cushing on a free-on-board basis, up from a discount of around $2.00-2.50 a barrel in the past two or three months.
Cusiana remains more expensive, fetching around 75-80 cents a barrel under WTI from a discount of $1.30-$1.40 in July on an fob basis.

Aside from the quality differences, Santa Barbara's relative cheapness is due to refiners' lack of familiarity with it and a worry that it might deteriorate in quality because it is currently run through the same pipeline as Venezuela's heavier Mesa crude, traders said.

Among the U.S. refiners that have picked up Santa Barbara crude in recent months are Crown, Mapco, Murphy and Marathon. BP Oil, British Petroleum's U.S. subsidiary, also has run the crude, while at least one other European refiner with U.S. operations is considering substituting some Brent for Santa Barbara, traders say.
Santa Barbara is produced from four fields, Musipn, Carito, El Tejero and Santa Barbara, located in northern Monagas state in eastern Venezuela near the prolific Furrial trend.
Current Santa Barbara production of around 130,000 barrels per day (bpd) is expected to climb to 140,000 bpd in the near term, a PDVSA spokesman says.
Corpoven produces about one million barrels per day (bpd) of oil, out of total Venezuelan output of more than three million bpd.
